name: Hallucination Risks in Clinical Content
blurb: Why generative AI output needs verification in trials.
title: Hallucination Risks in Clinical Content
answer: General purpose language models can produce convincing but false clinical content. Researchers showed a model could fabricate a plausible clinical trial dataset in minutes, and studies of generated references found large shares invented or inaccurate. In trial documents every claim must trace to source data.

reading.body:
General purpose language models can fabricate convincing clinical content, so no generated claim in a trial document should be accepted without a trace to source data.

Two documented results establish the pattern. A model produced a fake but plausible clinical trial dataset in minutes. Separately, 47 percent of references it generated were fabricated and another 46 percent were inaccurate, meaning roughly nine in ten were unusable as citations.

Trial documents are held to a different standard than drafts. Every claim must trace to source data, so a fabricated reference is not a stylistic flaw but a defect that invalidates the document it appears in. The recommended control follows from that: retrieval tied to the team's own documents, with citations to source records, and no unsourced generated facts accepted.

The data covers two 2023 findings and a verification practice. It does not measure how often these failures reach submitted trial documents, does not compare models, and does not address whether retrieval eliminates fabrication rather than reducing it.

sections.body: Use retrieval tied to your own documents and require citations to source records; never accept unsourced generated facts.

developments.text: Researchers in JAMA Ophthalmology showed a large language model could generate a fake but convincing clinical trial dataset.
A study found 47 percent of references produced by ChatGPT were fabricated and a further 46 percent inaccurate.
